Assess sensitivity of a fitted mixture model to initialisation

Source: R/sensitivity.R
sensitivity.Rd

sensitivity() evaluates how consistently a fitted mixture model is recovered from different random initialisations. Mixture-model estimation can converge to different local maxima, yielding different class assignments for the same data and model specification. Examining this dependence on initialisation helps assess the numerical reliability of the solution being interpreted.

The function repeats estimation under several random seeds and compares the resulting likelihood values and class assignments with the reference fit. Class labels are aligned before assignments are compared. By considering likelihood and classification agreement together, the analysis shows whether repeated searches recover a comparable fit and whether they assign the same observations to the same classes.

Results include convergence status, log likelihood, and classification agreement for each refit. Similar likelihood values are grouped using a specified tolerance. The data and model specification remain fixed throughout the analysis.

Usage

sensitivity(
  x,
  data = NULL,
  seeds = 1:10,
  n_starts = NULL,
  max_iter = NULL,
  tol = NULL,
  tolerance = NULL,
  cores = 1L
)

Arguments

x

The reference fit: a multilpa() model, an lta() model, or a growth mixture (mixture_regression() with random). A fit_staged() result varies the second-stage starts while holding its first-stage measurement solution fixed. A directly fitted model with measurement blocks held fixed is refused (latents_unsupported_sensitivity), because its original free starting values are not retained. A membership-covariate fit raises latents_unsupported_sensitivity. For an lta() fit, agreement is the share of occasions given the same profile, after matching the refit's profiles on the measurement; for a growth mixture it is the share of persons given the same class, after matching the refit's classes by their posterior memberships of the fitted persons.

data

Optional for a multilpa() fit or a growth mixture, which carry the columns they were built from. Required for an lta() fit (latents_bad_argument otherwise). It must be the data the model was fitted to, in its original row order; shared identifier and indicator columns are checked against the fit (latents_bad_inference_data).

seeds

At least two distinct integer seeds accepted by set.seed(). Default 1:10. Invalid values raise latents_bad_argument. Reusing the reference seed reproduces its initialisation when the other fitting controls are unchanged.

n_starts

Starts per refit. Defaults to the number the reference fit used.

max_iter, tol

Passed to each refit. Default to the reference fit's (for a fit that does not record them, to the defaults of the function that fitted it).

tolerance

Maximum log-likelihood difference for grouping refits. Each group is anchored at its highest log likelihood and spans no more than tolerance. Defaults to the reference fit's replication tolerance, 1e-6 per observed value.

cores

Number of processor cores (default 1). The seeds are refitted in parallel, one seed per worker at a time, each refit on one core. Every refit sets its own seed, so the result is identical to cores = 1. Workers are forked processes on macOS and Linux, and a socket cluster on Windows and on macOS with Apple's Accelerate BLAS, as in multilpa(); socket workers load the installed copy of the package. More cores than seeds are not used.

Value

A data.frame of class latents_sensitivity (which plot() draws), one row per seed, with columns seed, log_likelihood, converged, iterations, optimum (1 for the group containing the highest attained log likelihood, 2 for the next lower group, and so on), best (whether this seed reached optimum 1) and agreement (the proportion of classified observations given the same profile as the reference fit, after label matching). For profile and transition models, this uses observations included in both fits under their drop_empty settings. A failed refit has NA in every column except seed. The optimum and best columns group attained likelihood values without filtering on convergence; inspect converged before interpreting them as evidence of replicated maxima.

as.data.frame() returns a plain data.frame. plot() accepts main and subtitle and returns a ggplot object showing each refit's log-likelihood difference from the best converged refit and its classification agreement with the reference fit. Unfinished refits are distinguished from converged maxima; if none converged, the highest observed log likelihood is the reference instead.

Details

Replication across seeds complements replication across starts within one fit. Each refit uses the reference fit's estimation controls unless alternatives are supplied.

A seed whose refit fails gives a row with NA estimates, and a latents_sensitivity_dropped warning reports how many seeds failed.

Interpretation

Consistent results across converged refits support numerical reproducibility, but do not guarantee a global maximum or establish the validity of the model. Similar likelihood values alone do not imply identical parameter estimates. The analysis assesses sensitivity to initialisation, rather than uncertainty arising from sampling or model selection.

References

Hipp, J. R., & Bauer, D. J. (2006). Local solutions in the estimation of growth mixture models. Psychological Methods, 11, 36–53.

See also

enumerate_classes() to vary the number of classes, and parameter_inference() for uncertainty about the parameters of a single solution.

Examples

set.seed(7)
example_data <- data.frame(
  school = rep(seq_len(12), each = 10),
  score_a = c(rnorm(60, -1.5), rnorm(60, 1.5)),
  score_b = c(rnorm(60, -1), rnorm(60, 1))
)
fit <- multilpa(example_data, c("score_a", "score_b"), "school",
                n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 1, n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
sensitivity(fit, seeds = 1:3, n_starts = 3)
#>   seed log_likelihood converged iterations optimum best agreement
#> 1    1      -396.1633      TRUE          9       1 TRUE         1
#> 2    2      -396.1633      TRUE          9       1 TRUE         1
#> 3    3      -396.1633      TRUE          9       1 TRUE         1

# Growth mixtures are known for local solutions (Hipp and Bauer 2006).
growth <- mixture_regression(score ~ wave, data = subset(growth_scores, student <= 60),
                             n_classes = 2, id = "student", class_level = "group",
                             random = ~ 1, n_starts = 1, seed = 1)
sensitivity(growth, seeds = 1:2)
#>   seed log_likelihood converged iterations optimum best agreement
#> 1    1      -1175.788      TRUE         81       1 TRUE         1
#> 2    2      -1175.788      TRUE         81       1 TRUE         1
